summary: A standard method of encapsulating 802.2 packets on networks that support Novell's IPX protocol. It obsoletes earlier documents on carrying Internet packets over IPX, and allows multiple network protocols to be carried.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1132 says how to put Internet packets into Novell IPX packets so they can travel on an IPX network. It matters because one rule now covers several kinds of Internet traffic, including traffic that crosses IPX bridges.

questions: how does ip run over novell ipx
what is the mtu for ip over ipx
subtitle: How to carry IP, ARP and other 802.2 traffic inside Novell IPX datagrams, including across IPX bridges.

tldr.problem: Programs on an IPX network need an agreed way to carry Internet packets, and the earlier documents allowed only one protocol and no crossing of IPX bridges.
tldr.mechanism: IEEE 802.2 packets are encapsulated in IPX datagrams, so any protocol that uses 802.2 can run over IPX, and ARP maps an IP address to a 10-byte address of IPX network and node.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes the earlier documents and lets several network protocols share IPX. An IPX datagram holds at most 546 bytes, so the MTU is 538 bytes.

today: RFC 1132 is an Internet Standard, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Approach
sections.content:
The goal of RFC 1132 is compatible, interoperable transmission of Internet packets such as the Internet Protocol (IP), the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) and the Connectionless-mode Network Protocol (CLNP) over networks supporting Novell's Internet Packet Exchange Protocol (IPX). IPX is a proprietary standard developed by Novell and derived from Xerox's Internet Datagram Protocol.

The document defines the encapsulation of the IEEE 802.2 data link layer standard over IPX in terms of yet another 802.X physical layer standard, which allows IP datagrams to be transmitted as described in RFC 1042. It obsoletes earlier documents on the transmission of Internet packets over IPX and differs from them by allowing multiple network protocols over IPX and by allowing packets to go through IPX bridges.
sections.plainLanguage: It is one rule for putting any 802.2 traffic into IPX packets, so several kinds of protocol can share the same IPX network.

sections.title: Addresses and Byte Order
sections.content:
Internet Protocol addresses are mapped to 802.IPX addresses with the Address Resolution Protocol, in the same fashion as with other IEEE 802.X physical addresses. An 802.IPX physical address is 10 bytes rather than 2 or 6: the 4 bytes of the IPX network address followed by the 6 bytes of the IPX node address.

The byte transmission order is "big-endian". The IPX socket 0x8060 has been reserved by Novell for this protocol, and, like most IPX applications, this specification does not use the IPX checksum.
sections.plainLanguage: An address here is 10 bytes: the network number first, then the machine number. Bytes go on the wire largest first, and the IPX checksum is not used.

sections.title: Broadcast, Unicast and MTU
sections.content:
IPX packets may be broadcast by setting the IPX header Packet Type field to 0x14, the Destination Network field to the local network number, the Destination Node field to 0xffffff, and the Immediate Address field of the IPX Event Control Block to 0xffffff. For a unicast, Packet Type is set to 0x04, the Destination Network and Destination Node fields take the values found by address resolution, and the Immediate Address field is the physical address of the destination node or the appropriate IPX bridge.

The maximum data size of an IPX datagram is 546 bytes. The combined size of the 802.2 LLC and SNAP headers is 8 bytes, which gives a Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of 538 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending to one computer and sending to everyone use different settings on the envelope, and the envelope holds at most 538 bytes of payload.

sections.title: Implementation Notes
sections.content:
A typical IP over IPX packet is a physical header of N bytes, a 30-byte IPX header, an 8-byte 802.2 header, usually a 20-byte IP header, usually a 20-byte TCP header and up to 498 bytes of TCP data. Because the IPX interface insulates an application from the physical layer, 802.2 over IPX works over any physical medium. On workstations with an IPX programming interface, the only change needed was to allow address resolution cache entries larger than the hardware address length, so there is room for the immediate address of a possible intervening IPX bridge.

No implementations had been attempted on systems without an IPX interface, such as a dedicated router, but the RFC notes that no unicast packet is ever sent from one host to another without a prior broadcast packet from the other host, so the bridge's immediate address can be learned from the physical header of that broadcast. The memo does not address security.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet is a stack of labelled layers. A host can learn a bridge's address from the first broadcast it receives from the other side.
